analogy.p: Imagine you must go from one corner of a rectangular field to the opposite corner. You can walk along two sides (a then b) or cut straight across (c). The straight path is always shorter than the two sides together, but the surprising fact is exactly how much shorter: the square of the shortcut equals the squares of the two sides added. It maps well because the diagonal really is the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle formed by the sides. It breaks down if the corner is not a right angle, because then the shortcut length needs the cosine rule instead.

bullets: **Hypotenuse** = the longest side of a right-angled triangle, always **opposite the right angle**.
Formula: **c² = a² + b²** where c is the hypotenuse (this is NOT given on the Edexcel formula sheet, so you must memorise it).
The theorem is a statement about **areas**: the area of the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the areas of the squares on the other two sides.
It works in **any units** as long as all three sides use the same unit (convert first if needed).
Because the hypotenuse is the longest side, **c is always bigger than a and bigger than b**; use this to sense-check every answer.
The theorem can be used **both ways round**: to find a missing side, or (the converse) to test whether a triangle is right-angled.
Exam questions are often disguised: a 'ladder against a wall', a 'ship sailing north then east', a 'diagonal of a rectangle' all hide a right-angled triangle.
core.p: **Pythagoras' theorem** links the three side lengths of any **right-angled triangle**. It states that the **square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides**. In symbols, if the hypotenuse is c and the two shorter sides are a and b, then **a² + b² = c²**. It only works when the triangle contains a **90° angle**; for any other triangle you need the sine rule or cosine rule instead. It is one of the most heavily used results in the whole GCSE course because right-angled triangles appear inside rectangles, isosceles triangles, circles, coordinate grids and 3D shapes.

bullets: Find the **right-angle symbol** (small square) first; the hypotenuse is the side that does **not touch** the right angle.
If the triangle is rotated or upside-down, the hypotenuse is still opposite the right angle: it is **not necessarily the sloping or the bottom side**.
In a rectangle, the **diagonal** is the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle formed by two adjacent sides.
In an isosceles triangle, drawing the **perpendicular height** from the apex to the base creates two right-angled triangles with the slant side as hypotenuse.
Write the structure down as **hypotenuse² = side² + side²** before substituting numbers.
Label your diagram with the numbers given and put a **question mark** on the side you want, so you know whether to add or subtract.
If a diagram is 'not drawn accurately', do not measure it: use the numbers only.
core.p: The first and most important skill is to **spot the right angle and then the side opposite it**. That side is the hypotenuse and is the only one that gets squared on its own. The other two sides, called the **legs** or shorter sides, can be labelled a and b in either order because addition is commutative. Always sketch and label the triangle if the question gives only words, and mark the right angle with a small square. Many lost marks come from putting the wrong side as c, so a two second check at the start is worth it.

bullets: Method: **c² = a² + b²**, then **c = √(a² + b²)**.
Example: legs 5 and 12 give c² = 25 + 144 = 169, so **c = 13**.
Example: legs 6 and 9 give c² = 36 + 81 = 117, so c = √117 = **10.8** (3 s.f.), or exactly 3√13.
Always **square first, then add**: (a + b)² is NOT the same as a² + b².
Type √(25 + 144) with brackets on a calculator, or work out the sum first and then press the root key.
Do not round during the working: keep the full calculator value (or use the ANS key) until the final line.
Check: your answer must be **greater than the longer leg**; if not, you have subtracted by mistake.
core.h: Finding the hypotenuse (ADD then square root)
core.p: When the **longest side is unknown**, you know both shorter sides. Square each of them, **add** the results, and then take the **square root** to get c. The addition step is what makes the answer larger than either leg. The final square root step is the one students forget, leaving the answer as c² instead of c. Use the square root key on your calculator and give the answer to the accuracy asked for (usually 3 significant figures or 1 decimal place), or leave it exact as a surd if told to.

bullets: Rearrangement: **a² = c² − b²**, so **a = √(c² − b²)**.
Example: hypotenuse 17, leg 8: a² = 289 − 64 = 225, so **a = 15**.
Example: hypotenuse 10, leg 7: a² = 100 − 49 = 51, so a = √51 = **7.14** (3 s.f.).
Rule of thumb: **hypotenuse unknown = ADD; a shorter side unknown = SUBTRACT**.
The number under the square root must be **positive**: if you get a negative, you have swapped the sides.
Only take the **positive** square root for a length (a length cannot be negative).
Check by substituting back: a² + b² should equal c² (use your unrounded value).
core.h: Finding a shorter side (SUBTRACT then square root)
core.p: When the **hypotenuse is given** and you need one of the other sides, rearrange the theorem. Starting from a² + b² = c², subtract b² from both sides to get **a² = c² − b²**. So you square the hypotenuse, square the known leg, **subtract** the smaller square from the larger one, and then square root. This is the case where students most often add by mistake. The give-away is that the question tells you the longest side and asks for a shorter one, so the answer must be **smaller than the hypotenuse**.

bullets: Big square has side **(a + b)**, so area **(a + b)²**.
Each triangle has area **½ab**, so four triangles have total area **2ab**.
Arrangement 1: tilted square of side c in the middle: (a + b)² = c² + 2ab.
Expanding (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b², so a² + 2ab + b² = c² + 2ab.
Subtract 2ab from both sides: **a² + b² = c²**. This is a clean algebraic proof that fits a 4 mark 'show that' question.
The theorem is named after the Greek mathematician **Pythagoras**, but it was known to Babylonian, Indian and Chinese mathematicians earlier.
Visual check with a 3-4-5 triangle: squares of areas 9 and 16 together make a square of area 25 (see the first diagram).
core.h: Why the theorem works: the area proof
core.p: You may be asked to **prove** or explain Pythagoras, and understanding the reason makes it easier to remember. Draw a square of side (a + b) and place four copies of the right-angled triangle inside it in two different arrangements. In the first arrangement the leftover space is a tilted square of side c, so its area is c². In the second the leftover space is two squares of areas a² and b². Because the big square and the four triangles are identical in both pictures, the leftover areas must be equal, giving **c² = a² + b²**. This is a proof by **rearrangement of equal areas**.

bullets: If two sides match a known triple (e.g. 12 and 13 with 13 as hypotenuse), the third side is the missing member (5).
A triple must be **whole numbers**: 1.5, 2, 2.5 is a scaled version (×½ of 3, 4, 5) but is not itself a triple.
Triples are useful in **non-calculator** questions to give exact integer answers.
In the exam, writing c² = a² + b² and the numerical working is still needed for full marks even if you recognised the triple.
Not every right-angled triangle gives a triple: e.g. legs 1 and 1 give hypotenuse √2, which is irrational.
core.p: A **Pythagorean triple** is a set of three **positive whole numbers** that satisfy a² + b² = c². Learning the common ones saves time and lets you spot answers without a calculator, which is useful on the non-calculator paper. Any triple can be **scaled up** (multiplied by the same number) to give another triple, because multiplying every side by k multiplies every square by k². Spotting a triple also tells you a diagram is 'nice' and the answer should be an integer.

bullets: Test: does **(short)² + (short)² = (longest)²**? Always put the longest side on the right-hand side.
Example: sides 7, 24, 25: 7² + 24² = 49 + 576 = 625 = 25², so the triangle **is right-angled**.
Example: sides 6, 7, 10: 36 + 49 = 85 but 10² = 100, so 85 is less than 100: the triangle is **obtuse**, not right-angled.
Write a **conclusion**: 'Since 7² + 24² = 25², the triangle is right-angled (converse of Pythagoras).'
This is how builders check corners are square, using a **3-4-5 rope** (or 6-8-10).
If the sums are not equal you must still say what that means: 'not right-angled'.
The right angle is opposite the **longest** side.
core.h: The converse: proving a triangle is right-angled
core.p: The **converse of Pythagoras** says that if the sides of a triangle satisfy a² + b² = c² then the triangle **must** be right-angled, with the right angle opposite c. To test a triangle, take the **two shorter sides**, square and add them, and compare with the square of the **longest side**. If they are equal the triangle is right-angled; you must write a conclusion in words to earn the final mark. Higher tier extension: if a² + b² is **greater** than c² the triangle is acute (all angles less than 90°), and if it is **less** than c² the largest angle is obtuse.

bullets: Simplify a surd by pulling out the **largest square factor**: √72 = √(36 × 2) = 6√2.
Exact answers can include square roots: a right-angled triangle with legs 1 and 2 has hypotenuse **√5**.
If a question says 'Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures', **show the unrounded value first** (e.g. 10.8167…) then the rounded one.
Give lengths in the correct units and **area in square units** (cm², m²).
Check with estimation: √117 lies between √100 = 10 and √121 = 11, so about 10.8 is believable.
On the calculator paper, store the unrounded value with the **ANS** or memory key to avoid cumulative rounding error.
Rationalising a denominator may be needed when a surd ends up in a fraction (link to Number).
core.p: Questions on the non-calculator paper or marked 'give your answer in surd form' expect a **simplified surd** rather than a decimal. If c² = 50, then c = √50 = 5√2 because 50 = 25 × 2 and √25 = 5. When a decimal is asked for, the standard accuracy is **3 significant figures** unless the question specifies otherwise, and answers must carry the correct **units**. Never round until the final step, and make sure that the rounded answer still obeys the rule that the hypotenuse is the longest side.

bullets: **Ladder**: ladder length = hypotenuse; foot distance and height up the wall are the legs. Ladder 6.5 m, foot 2.5 m from wall: height² = 42.25 − 6.25 = 36, so height = **6 m**.
**Ship or walker**: two perpendicular journeys (north and east) give legs; the direct distance is the hypotenuse.
**Rectangle diagonal**: for an 8 cm by 15 cm rectangle, diagonal = √(64 + 225) = √289 = **17 cm**.
**Perimeter and area** problems: find the missing side first with Pythagoras, then use it (e.g. area of a trapezium needs its height).
**Compound shapes**: split into rectangles and right-angled triangles, then find hidden lengths.
Always **answer the question asked**: if asked for the perimeter, add all sides after finding the missing one.
Give a sentence answer with units in context questions (e.g. 'The ladder reaches 6 m up the wall').
Real-life context may give bearings; a bearing of 090° or 000° gives perpendicular legs (link to Bearings).
core.h: Pythagoras in context: ladders, ships and diagonals
core.p: Most exam marks come from **applying** the theorem to real situations. The skill is to read the story, **draw a right-angled triangle**, label the known lengths, decide which side is the hypotenuse, and only then calculate. A ladder leaning on a vertical wall on horizontal ground forms a right angle at the base of the wall, so the ladder is the hypotenuse. A ship that sails due north then due east forms a right angle at the turning point, so the straight-line distance back is the hypotenuse. A rectangle's diagonal splits it into two right-angled triangles.

bullets: Isosceles triangle 13, 13, 10: half base = 5, so h² = 13² − 5² = 169 − 25 = 144, **h = 12**, and area = ½ × 10 × 12 = **60 cm²** (see diagram).
Equilateral triangle side 10: half base 5, h² = 100 − 25 = 75, **h = √75 = 5√3 ≈ 8.66**; area = ½ × 10 × 5√3 = **25√3 ≈ 43.3**.
General equilateral height: **h = (√3/2) × side**; area = (√3/4) × side².
The perpendicular from the apex of an isosceles triangle **bisects the base** (symmetry/congruent triangles).
Use this to find the area of any isosceles triangle when you only know the three sides.
The same idea finds the **height of a trapezium** or parallelogram if the slanted side and horizontal overhang are known.
Link: the 30-60-90 triangle formed has sides in the ratio **1 : √3 : 2**, which leads to exact trig values.
core.h: Isosceles and equilateral triangles: finding the height
core.p: A very common Higher tier technique is to **split an isosceles triangle down the middle**. The line from the apex to the midpoint of the base is perpendicular to the base, so it creates two congruent right-angled triangles. Half the base is one leg, the perpendicular height is the other leg, and one of the equal sides is the hypotenuse. This lets you find the height, and therefore the area (½ × base × height). The same trick works for an equilateral triangle of side s, where the height is **(√3 / 2) × s**.

bullets: Sketch the points and the right-angled triangle to avoid sign errors.
The **midpoint** is a different formula: average the x's and y's; do not confuse the two.
Used to prove a triangle on a grid is **isosceles** (two equal distances) or **right-angled** (use the converse).
Link to **circles**: x² + y² = r² is Pythagoras applied to a point (x, y) at distance r from the origin.
Link to **vectors**: the magnitude of the vector (a, b) is √(a² + b²).
core.h: Distance between two points on a coordinate grid
core.p: The distance between two points is found by drawing a **right-angled triangle** whose hypotenuse joins them. The horizontal leg is the difference in x-coordinates and the vertical leg is the difference in y-coordinates. So the distance between (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂) is **d = √[(x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²]**. Because the differences are squared, it does not matter which point you subtract from which, and negative differences cause no trouble. This idea is also behind the length of a vector and the equation of a circle.

bullets: Chord of length 16 in a circle of radius 10: half chord 8, so distance from centre = √(100 − 64) = **6** (see diagram).
Tangent from an external point P to a circle centre O radius r: **tangent length = √(OP² − r²)**.
The radius to the midpoint of a chord is perpendicular to the chord (circle theorem).
Two tangents from the same point are equal in length.
A diameter has length 2r; an angle in a semicircle is 90°, so the triangle formed has the diameter as hypotenuse.
Always mark the **right angle** you are using and state the circle theorem that justifies it.
Link to Circle theorems: the reason for the right angle must be stated in a reasoned-proof question.
core.p: Right-angled triangles appear in circles in two main ways. First, the **perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects the chord**, so half the chord, the distance from the centre to the chord and the radius form a right-angled triangle with the radius as hypotenuse. Second, a **tangent is perpendicular to the radius** at the point of contact, so the radius, tangent length and the line from the external point to the centre form a right-angled triangle with the centre line as hypotenuse. Both give length problems that need only Pythagoras.

bullets: Example: sides x and x + 7 with hypotenuse 13: x² + (x + 7)² = 169 gives 2x² + 14x − 120 = 0, so x² + 7x − 60 = 0, (x + 12)(x − 5) = 0, **x = 5** (reject −12). The triangle is 5, 12, 13.
**Expand brackets properly**: (x + 3)² = x² + 6x + 9, not x² + 9.
Reject negative or impossible solutions and **explain why** in a word or two.
Surd answers can appear when the quadratic has irrational roots.
Strategy: label, choose the right-angled triangle, write the equation, solve, answer in context.
Link: Pythagoras with **trigonometry** (finding angles once all sides are known), **3D Pythagoras** (space diagonals) and **vectors** (magnitudes).
In proof questions, use only what the diagram tells you (e.g. 'angle in a semicircle') and state every reason.
core.p: At Higher tier the side lengths can be **algebraic expressions**, so Pythagoras produces an equation to solve, usually a quadratic. Substitute the expressions, expand carefully (remember (x + 7)² = x² + 14x + 49), collect terms to one side and solve by factorising or the quadratic formula. Reject any solution that makes a length **negative**. For multi-step problems, plan a route: find the missing side, then use it for a second calculation such as area, perimeter, trigonometry or another application of the theorem.

exam: **Command words**: 'Calculate' means show working and a numerical answer; 'Show that' means you must arrive at the given result with every step visible; 'Work out' needs a method; 'Prove' needs a reasoned conclusion.
**1 to 2 marks**: a direct calculation of a missing side. Mark scheme: M1 for a correct equation such as x² = 8² + 15², A1 for 17.
**3 marks**: a context question (ladder, ship). Typical marks: M1 for a right-angled triangle method, M1 for correct squares and add/subtract, A1 for the answer with units.
**4 marks**: multi-step (find a height then area, or perimeter). The answer line often needs units and the correct rounding.
**6 marks (QWC style, Higher)**: algebraic Pythagoras or reasoning with circle theorems. Structure: diagram, equation, expansion, quadratic solution, rejection of invalid root, final answer.
Always **write the formula and substitute**; M marks are awarded for the method even if the arithmetic slips.
On non-calculator papers look for **triples** and simplify surds rather than writing decimals.
For 'prove it is right-angled' questions, the model phrase is: **'a² + b² = c² so by the converse of Pythagoras the triangle is right-angled'**.
Sketch a triangle for every word problem: examiners often award a mark for a correct diagram or labelled lengths.
Check that your answer is **sensible**: hypotenuse the longest side, a shorter side shorter than the hypotenuse.
If a question gives 'diagram not drawn accurately', rely on the numbers, not on measuring.

mistakes.r: When the hypotenuse is known, subtract: a² = c² − b². The answer must be smaller than the hypotenuse.
mistakes.w: Adding the squares when finding a shorter side (e.g. 17² + 8²)

mistakes.r: Take the square root at the end: c = √169 = 13. Show the final square root step.
mistakes.w: Stopping at c² = 169 and writing 169 as the length

mistakes.r: Pythagoras only works when there is a 90° angle; otherwise use the sine or cosine rule.
mistakes.w: Using the theorem on a triangle with no right angle

mistakes.r: Square each side first, then add: a² + b². Expanding (a + b)² gives a² + 2ab + b².
The hypotenuse is always opposite the right angle; identify the right angle first.
mistakes.w: Calling the longest-looking or bottom side the hypotenuse

mistakes.r: Keep full calculator values until the end and round once to 3 s.f. (or as asked).
mistakes.w: Rounding too early and getting an inaccurate final answer

mistakes.r: State 'Since a² + b² = c², the triangle is right-angled (converse of Pythagoras)'; the conclusion earns the final mark.
mistakes.w: Testing a right-angled triangle but not writing a conclusion

mistakes.r: Always include correct units; area is in square units.
mistakes.w: Forgetting units, or giving area in cm instead of cm²

mistakes.r: Reject negative solutions because lengths must be positive, and say why.
mistakes.w: Keeping both ±5 as lengths in an algebra question

summary: Know and apply Pythagoras' theorem (a² + b² = c²) to find missing sides of right-angled triangles in 2D, to test whether a triangle is right-angled (the converse), and to solve problems in context, on coordinate grids, in isosceles triangles and in circles. It underpins trigonometry, vectors, circle equations and 3D problems, so it is secure marks on every Edexcel Higher paper.

terms.d: The longest side of a right-angled triangle, opposite the right angle.
A triangle with one angle of exactly 90°.
In a right-angled triangle, the square on the hypotenuse is equal to the sum of the squares on the other two sides: a² + b² = c².
If a² + b² = c² for the sides of a triangle, then the triangle is right-angled, with the right angle opposite side c.
Three positive integers a, b, c that satisfy a² + b² = c², such as 3, 4, 5.
The inverse of squaring; √x is the positive number which, multiplied by itself, gives x.
An irrational root that cannot be written exactly as a fraction, such as √2, left in root form to be exact.
Either of the two sides of a right-angled triangle that form the right angle.
At right angles (90°) to a given line.
The shortest distance from a vertex to the opposite side (or its extension), measured at 90° to that side.
A straight line joining two points on the circumference of a circle.
A straight line that touches a circle at one point and is perpendicular to the radius at that point.
A triangle with two equal sides and two equal angles.
The digits of a number that carry meaning about its precision, counted from the first non-zero digit.

worked.ans: The ladder reaches 6 m up the wall.
worked.q: A ladder 6.5 m long leans against a vertical wall. The foot of the ladder is 2.5 m from the wall on horizontal ground. How high up the wall does the ladder reach? (3 marks)
steps: The ladder is the hypotenuse, c = 6.5; the foot distance is one leg, b = 2.5; the height h is the other leg.

worked.ans: AB = 10 units; triangle ABC is right-angled at C because AC is horizontal and BC is vertical (also 6² + 8² = 10²).
worked.q: A(1, 2) and B(7, 10) are points on a coordinate grid. Work out the length AB. Then state whether triangle ABC with C(7, 2) is right-angled and give a reason. (4 marks)
steps: C(7, 2) shares y with A and x with B, so AC is horizontal and BC is vertical, meeting at 90°.

worked.q: The sides of a right-angled triangle are x, x + 7 and 13, where 13 is the hypotenuse. Find x and show your working. (5 marks)
steps: Reject x = −12 because a length cannot be negative.
